extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students, and fans of film/literature/television interested in genre studies
extracted.subtask_description: Describe and characterize the comedy‑horror (horror‑comedy) genre across literature, film, and television, including its types, devices, historical trends, and typical tones. Useful for genre analysis, criticism, or creating works that blend horror and comedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: combination of comedy and horror
rubrics_metrics.description: "Comedy horror (also called horror comedy) is a literary, television and film genre that combines elements of comedy and horror fiction.",
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applies across media (literature, TV, film). The defining feature is the deliberate blending of humorous and frightening elements rather than pure horror or pure comedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three principal types
rubrics_metrics.description: "Comedy horror has been described as having three types: 'black comedy, parody and spoof.'"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These three categories are commonly used to classify works in the genre: black comedy that mixes dark themes with humor; parody that explicitly imitates and mocks horror conventions; and spoof which broadly lampoons horror tropes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of parody and spoofing horror clichés
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy horror can parody or subtly spoof horror clichés as its main source of humour or use those elements to take a story in a different direction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parody/spoof may be the central comedic strategy (e.g., Scary Movie-style direct lampooning) or a subtler device that retools clichés to produce both scares and laughs. Examples cited include films that reference or invert familiar horror tropes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gallows (dark) humour as a common element
rubrics_metrics.description: "In comedy horror film, gallows humor is a common element."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gallows humor lets audiences laugh at frightening or taboo subjects. The article notes this gives viewers "the permission to laugh at your fears, to whistle past the cinematic graveyard and feel secure in the knowledge that the monsters can't get you." This device influences tone and audience response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance between horror and comedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Works vary in where they place emphasis between horror and comedy; early experiments were often unbalanced, later works aimed for more sophisticated mixes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A successful comedy‑horror often achieves an effective balance so both scares and laughs function. Historical notes: early films (e.g., One Exciting Night) were not well-balanced, while later films improved the blending of genres.

rubrics_metrics.name: Slapstick plus gore/body horror blending (1980s–1990s trend)
rubrics_metrics.description: The 1980s marked a shift toward more extreme and graphic horror comedies featuring elaborate practical effects and exaggerated gore, merging body horror with absurd humor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This style emphasizes physical, often gross-out comedy combined with practical effects (examples: An American Werewolf in London, Evil Dead II, Braindead). It also includes titles that balance fantasy-horror elements with wider-audience comedic tone (Gremlins, Beetlejuice).

rubrics_metrics.name: Meta‑horror and self‑awareness (2000s–present)
rubrics_metrics.description: Horror comedies in the 21st century frequently incorporate meta-commentary on the horror genre itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Scary Movie (direct parody of specific films), Shaun of the Dead (comedic homage to zombie cinema), Cabin in the Woods (self-aware deconstruction of archetypes). Meta-humor often comments on genre conventions while still engaging with them narratively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social satire via horror‑comedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Recent horror comedies have used the blend to deliver social critique—for example, Get Out blended psychological horror with dark humor to critique racial dynamics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The genre can be a vehicle for satire and commentary on social issues (race, class, generational divides). Other examples cited: Ready or Not and Bodies Bodies Bodies used horror-comedy to comment on class/generational divides.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical/literary roots and tonal juxtaposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Horror and comedy have been associated since early horror novels; works like Washington Irving's "The Legend of Sleepy Hollow" made readers "laugh one moment and scream the next."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Literary precedent includes Mary Shelley's Frankenstein parodies, Poe's placement of humor and horror on a continuum, and nineteenth-century black humor in horror stories. The key device is juxtaposing laughter and fear within the same work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Television forms and stylistic variety
rubrics_metrics.description: Horror comedy on television ranges from classic sitcoms (The Munsters, The Addams Family) to gory slapstick (Ash vs Evil Dead), mockumentaries (What We Do in the Shadows, Wellington Paranormal), and animated entries (Beetlejuice, Invader Zim).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: TV allows a wide variety of tones and formats for comedy-horror—sitcom, serialized horror-comedy, mockumentary, animation—each altering how comedic and horrific elements are deployed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variation in primary function: comedy-first vs horror-first works
rubrics_metrics.description: Not all titles blend equally—some function primarily as comedy with horror references (e.g., Scary Movie), while others are horror films with strong comedic elements or homage (e.g., Shaun of the Dead).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This distinction affects audience expectations and marketing: a comedy-first work uses horror mainly as material to parody; a horror-first work uses comedic elements to modulate tension, provide relief, or deepen satirical aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taxonomy and related subgenres
rubrics_metrics.description: Related categories and subgenres include zombie comedy (a subgenre involving zombies) and black comedy; the article links comedy-horror to adjacent genres such as satire, parody, fantastique and more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understanding related subgenres helps classify works and set expectations (e.g., "zombie comedy" signals particular conventions). The article situates comedy-horror within broader genre taxonomies (film, literature, television) and lists many related forms.
